title: Security log forwarder design: customer requirements and adapter guide
body:
Purpose and scope:

This working doc captures a practical pattern for a lightweight security-log forwarder and adapter interface that teams and customers can use to reliably export audit and evidentiary logs to third-party SIEMs (Splunk, Datadog, Azure Sentinel). It combines operational constraints, RBAC-driven filter controls, audit schema expectations, evidence automation hooks, and connector reliability requirements. The goal is a single, opinionated forwarder + adapter model that balances low-latency streaming with tamper-evident delivery and customer-side control over data scope.

Audience:
- Internal: security, compliance, infra, SRE, product (private deployments)
- External: customer security engineers, SOC integrators, managed service vendors

High-level pattern summary:
- Forwarder (lightweight client): runs in customer VPC or in Redwood-managed forwarder fleet. Responsible for batching, envelope signing, local persistence (small write-ahead log), backpressure handling, and format normalization into the export envelope.
- Adapter/connector: infra component that translates the envelope to destination-specific transport (Splunk HEC, Datadog HTTP intake, Azure Event Hubs/Log Analytics / Sentinel connector). The adapter implements retries, rate-limit handling, and field mapping.
- Control plane: central service (private or hosted) where RBAC v2 policies determine which audit streams a tenant is allowed to export and what transformations are permitted (redaction, field scrubbing, route overrides).
- Evidence automation: an optional hook that produces signed evidence bundles for compliance requests (time-limited, integrity-signed manifests pointing to archived payloads).

Customer requirements checklist (recommended minimums):
1) Data scope & filtering
   - Customer must declare the intended export categories: auth events, admin actions, model inference events, billing traces.
   - RBAC v2 export filters: exports are gated by roles defined in RBAC v2. Only principals with export_allow permission may request or reconfigure export routes.
   - Field-level allowlist/denylist: customers can declare allowed fields per export target. Forwarder enforces denylist before sending.

2) Delivery guarantees and SLAs
   - Best-effort streaming with at-least-once semantics by default.
   - Optional exactly-once upstack using idempotency keys and dedupe windows for customers who need strict audit accounting.
   - Local persistence: forwarder must persist up to 24 hours of unsent data in case of network outage (configurable).

3) Security and integrity
   - Envelope signing: forwarder signs each batch with tenant key (KMS-backed or customer HSM) and includes signature metadata in the envelope.
   - TLS + mTLS for control plane and adapter communications.
   - Replay protection: sequence IDs and monotonic counters in envelopes; adapters reject out-of-order or replays beyond configured window.

4) Privacy and redaction
   - Redaction hooks executed locally in forwarder prior to transmission. Redaction policy is a customer artifact (YAML/JSON) authorized by RBAC v2.
   - PII classification helpers included to identify common fields (email, ip, token, ssn).

5) Observability and debugging
   - Forwarder exposes per-route metrics (latency, success rate, queue depth) and logs with minimal PII.
   - Trace IDs preserved across export for root-cause tracing (correlate with request-level traces in Redwood Console).

6) Evidence automation and lawful audit requests
   - Evidence bundle: when triggered (manual or automated), forwarder creates a compressed, signed bundle that contains: manifest.json, exported-records.ndjson (reference to stored objects), and signature.asc.
   - Retention controls: customer must specify retention windows for archived evidence (30/90/365 days).

Connector / adapter spec (behavioral):
- Generic envelope intake: adapter receives our standard export envelope (see sample below). Adapter responsibility: unwrap, validate signature, map fields to destination schema, apply destination-specific batching and retry policy.
- Idempotency and dedupe: adapters maintain a short-lived dedupe cache keyed by envelope-id or record-id to prevent duplicate ingestion on retries.
- Error classification: adapters must map HTTP failures to retryable vs permanent categories. Rate-limit (429) and 5xx are retryable with backoff; 4xx client errors surface to control plane and owner.
- Backpressure and congestion: adapters report backpressure signals to the forwarder via a control ACK channel (for managed scenarios) or HTTP 429 responses (for direct-forwarder-to-adapter). Forwarder reduces publish rate and increases batching when backpressure observed.

Field mapping guidance (destination specifics):
- Splunk HEC: flatten important envelope fields into event JSON, set "sourcetype" to "redwood:audit:v1". Include "tenant_id", "stream", "envelope_id", "seq_id" as top-level metadata fields.
- Datadog: emit as events with tags: "tenant:<id>", "stream:<name>", and submit large arrays as separate events with parent_id to preserve grouping. Use Datadog intake max payload guidance to avoid truncation.
- Azure Sentinel / Log Analytics: map to custom log schema, create a "RedwoodAudit_CL" table with columns for envelope_id_s, tenant_id_s, event_time_t, record_s, signature_s. Ensure special characters are escaped per Kusto ingestion rules.

Operational patterns and anti-patterns:
- Do: keep redaction and PII removal local to the forwarder.
- Do: use short-lived, rekeyed signing keys to minimize blast radius of key compromise.
- Do: provide a "dry-run" mode that validates mapping without transmitting customer data (useful for SOC onboarding).
- Don’t: rely on the adapter to redact; adapters should not be trusted for policy enforcement in customer-managed environments.

RBAC v2 interplay and enforcement model:
- Export policies are represented as RBAC v2 objects: export-target, export-policy, export-operator.
- Example rule: role "security-analyst" has "export_target.read" but not "export_target.configure". This prevents analysts from changing field allowlists while permitting them to pull exports.
- Audit trails: any change to export configuration is recorded in the audit log with before/after snapshots and stored as an immutable entry. These change events are included in evidence bundles.

Sample export envelope (ndjson-style inside the body for reference):
{
  "envelope_id": "env-20241129-0001",
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "seq_id_start": 987654321,
  "records": [
    { "record_id": "r-0001", "stream": "auth", "ts": "2024-11-29T15:22:10Z", "payload": {"user":"alice@example.com","action":"login","success":true} },
    { "record_id": "r-0002", "stream": "admin", "ts": "2024-11-29T15:22:11Z", "payload": {"actor":"svc-deployer","action":"deploy","resource":"model-x"} }
  ],
  "signature": "MEUCIQD...base64sig...",
  "signature_meta": { "alg": "RSA-PSS", "key_id": "kms:projects/p/keys/exp-2024" },
  "backfill": false
}

Note: the actual file transmitted may be ndjson where each record is an entry to keep memory usage low; envelope metadata is included as a preceding header line. Adapters should be tolerant of both ndjson and compact JSON envelopes.

Onboarding checklist for product/Sales/CS: (what to collect from customer)
- Customer export use-case and target SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel).
- Required retention and evidence retention windows.
- RBAC mapping document: list of roles and who can configure exports.
- Redaction policy (customer-provided or bank-of-common-redactions).
- Network topology: whether forwarder runs in-customer-vpc or Redwood-managed.
- KMS/HSM choice for signing keys.

Developer notes and testing matrix:
- Integration tests: validate envelope signature verification, replay detection, field-denylist enforcement, and idempotency behavior.
- Load test: emulate 10k events/sec per tenant with mixed record sizes; validate local buffer eviction and adapter backpressure behavior.
- Chaos tests: simulate adapter slowdowns and verify forwarder persists and recovers without data loss.

Open questions / decision log (WIP):
- Exactly-once semantics cost: should we make dedupe optional per tenant or default to at-least-once? (proposal: optional exactly-once for enterprise contracts).
- Evidence archival storage: S3 vs customer-managed archive — which is default for Private deployments?
- Field-level encryption: do we support transparent field encryption within envelope payloads for highly sensitive fields?

Appendix: short FAQ
Q: Can a customer restrict exports by tag (e.g., prod vs staging)?
A: Yes, export filters support arbitrary metadata tags; RBAC policies can gate tag-level exports.

Q: What happens if an adapter signals backpressure repeatedly?
A: Forwarder will increase batching, apply exponential backoff, escalate to control plane for route failover, and, if configured, switch to archive-mode where payloads are stored rather than dropped.

Q: How are audit changes protected from forgery?
A: Export configuration changes are signed by operator identity (RBAC credential) and recorded as immutable audit entries; the evidence bundle includes hash chains to prove ordering.

---
Author notes: this is a pragmatic, customer-facing working doc intended for early engineering + security review. After internal signoff we will produce a shorter onboarding checklist and a sample Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel connector repo template under the telemetry-forwarder mono-repo.
